I am just pointing out that the act specifically says it is the function and duty of the board of transport commissioners, of its own volition, to look into this question and find out whether or not Toronto can qualify for steam suburban service on the same basis as Montreal. I am glad to see Montreal has that service. The only regret is that the board of transport commissioners should be required to carry out the law, and where similar facts exist, similar service should be granted.

Following up what the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has said, may I ask the minister if there is a difference between the surburban service of Montreal and that which is given to the Toronto area?
Yes, there is.
What is the distinction? I have just been relying on what the member has said, but I should like to know what the distinction is between the two cities.
There is such a service between the city of Montreal and the outlying districts and I understand there is not in Toronto.
That is a steam suburban service?

On that point, there is a suburban service. Dealing with the point raised by my hon. friend, I have to make the same answer as I made to a question a short time ago; that is a matter for the board to decide upon an application to them. The question is: Is that what the hon. gentleman wants, a steam suburban service for the city of Toronto? If it is, I shall be the most astonished man in the world, because the railways have been trying in the last few years to get away from steam locomotives. The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) has on the order paper a bill the purpose of which is to eliminate smoke. He wants the railways to install certain equipment in roundhouses in the city of Toronto to eliminate smoke. We have that request from one gentleman and a request for a Steam suburban service from another gentleman.
I want cheap rates.

If it is cheap rates, that is clearly a matter for the board.. If it is a steam suburban service, I think, before one could answer yes to that, more careful consideration would have to be given. I know
(Mr. Church.]
the railways are modernizing their equipment and eliminating steam locomotives.
They are getting diesels?

Yes, diesels. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company announced a policy some time ago to the effect that no more steam locomotives would be purchased. They are directing their attention exclusively towards diesels. I believe I am safe in saying that is substantially the policy of the Canadian National Railways.
Coming back to the question of rates, if that is the question that is being brought to the attention of the house, J must say it is a matter for the board to decide upon application to it.

As the committee knows, the board of transport commissioners recently handed down a decision on the application of the railways for an increase of twenty per cent and also on a rehearing of the former application. The general result of the decision was an increase in rates of 29 per cent. In giving judgment, the board stated that was only a temporary increase, and that they would give further consideration to the application of the railways for a 20 per cent increase after the two inquiries which are being undertaken have been completed.
As we all know, there is a royal commission on transportation which has been sitting for some months. In addition, the board of transport commissioners was ordered to make a general inquiry into the whole freight rate structure, and particularly into the question of discrimination. Can the minister tell us when those two inquiries are to be completed? It would appear that the board's inquiry has not yet got under way. The result is that it will probably be some time before they make a finding. This is particularly important to the western provinces and to the eastern provinces because, with the recent increase in rates, the discrimination was made just that much worse than it had been before. Apparently there can be no remedy for the discrimination until these two reports are in.

It is of course rather difficult to tell the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra the exact time at which these two investigations will be completed. The royal commission has had sittings in western Canada, has gone down to Newfoundland and is now on its way back; in fact, it is back. When it will move to the other provinces, if it so decides, I am not in a position to say. I hardly think they will have completed the hearings before the month of December, and it will be some

time after that before they are able to compile the tremendous amount of evidence before them and bring down their conclusions. Whether it would be a year from now or not, I am not in a position to say. If I had had the opportunity of consulting with the chairman, I might be able to give the hon. member some idea with regard to the time; but it will certainly not be in the immediate future.
Dealing with order in council P.C. 1487, on the general equalization of freight rates-
The minister is now dealing with the inquiry to be undertaken by the board of transport commissioners as distinguished from that undertaken by the royal commission?

I am dealing with P.C. 1487 which authorized the board of transport commissioners to set up an inquiry to deal with the general matter of the equalization of freight rates. That has been under way now for almost a year, and at the moment the board is going into the study of the waybill, which is an important factor in arriving at the matter of discrimination. It will be some months still-in fact, I think it will go into next year-before they are able to conclude their findings on the waybill study. As to when they will bring in their report, I am afraid I cannot give my hon. friend any definite date, except to say that it will not be soon.
Will public hearings be held by the board of transport commissioners in carrying out this general inquiry, or is that merely a study being undertaken by them?
Yes, it is a study being undertaken by the board.

Last spring we understood that the board would be holding public hearings having to do with this question of discrimination. Surely, on an important matter like that, they are not going to make their findings without giving the provinces an opportunity to make representations.

That is a matter which the chairman, in conjunction with the other members of the board, will have to decide. I do not know what he intends to do. He is the court and he is the one who must decide whether hearings will be held across the country or not. I cannot speak for him at this time without consultation with him. The waybill subject matter is one of study; it is not one which would call for a public hearing. The matter of the mountain differential was one which did, and hearings were held. I think that is a matter for the discretion of the chairman.
Supply-Transport

As I understood it, the provinces were asking for an opportunity to make representations on this whole question of discrimination. The board of transport commissioners has wide power under the order in council. When that order in council was passed, was it not the intention of the government that the board should hold public hearings?

The board has already held one public hearing. Having decided to remove the mountain differential in the British Columbia area, they then thought the next procedure was to make a study of the waybill. Having done that, what they intend to do afterwards is something I am not able to say. As to the intention of the government,
I have made statements from time to time, and the order in council is there. I do not think I should elaborate further.
Perhaps the minister could tell the committee at a later date what plan the board have in mind.
Yes. I shall be glad to consult with the chairman of the board and at a later date to make a statement as to his intention.
This is an exceedingly important matter.
Unquestionably it is an exceedingly important matter.
I would ask that the minister allow the item to stand.
Surely we can discuss this matter on the general item.
No-

Just a minute. If it is the-intention of the committee to let every item such as this stand, we shall never get on. At my hon. friend's request we have let item 453 stand, so that we could discuss general matters. I tell my friend now that he will have an opportunity to deal with this matter under item 453. I should think that would be sufficient.

I have run into difficulties before over some plan of this kind. It is now six o'clock. This information for which I have asked the minister is most important, and I would suggest that the item be allowed to stand.
Item stands.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It being six o'clock, shall I report progress and ask leave to sit again?
Progress reported.

Business of the House BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow is private members' day.

In view of our experience today, I should like to ask the minister this question. If tomorrow we find that private members' notices of motions stand in such numbers and as frequently as they did this afternoon, what will the government business be following disposal of them?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Public bills and orders come first.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have some bills under study in committee which we could take up, or we could revert to estimates of the Department of Agriculture or of the Department of Transport.

Would the business of
tomorrow include the bill to amend the Supreme Court Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Probably; and the bill to amend the Exchequer Court Act and the one to amend the Department of Justice Act.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, October 6, 1949
